instruments.title: Information Technology Act, 2000
instruments.status: In force. s.43A stays in force until DPDP Act s.44(2) commences on 2027-05-13
instruments.summary: Core cyber law. Computer misuse, identity theft and personation offences, privacy violation, obscene content, blocking powers and intermediary safe harbour. No AI-specific provisions.
instruments.note: Enforcement date from India Code. Section list and s.43A end date supplied by the project owner; Gazette copy not checked. s.79A (Examiner of Electronic Evidence) added in v0.2; section contents otherwise summarised from researcher knowledge.

instruments.title: IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021
instruments.provisions: Rule 3(1)(b) due diligence (substituted by G.S.R. 794(E), 28 Oct 2022)
instruments.summary: Due-diligence duties for intermediaries, including not hosting listed unlawful or knowingly false content. Invoked by MeitY against an AI chatbot answer in Feb 2024.
instruments.note: G.S.R. numbers and dates supplied by the project owner. URL is a copy in Gazette layout on a nic.in court website, found by web search; it has not been opened (host blocked from the AI-assisted session's sandbox) and is not the egazette.gov.in original. Missing for 'yes': open and confirm a Gazette copy of G.S.R. 139(E), or replace this link with the egazette.gov.in original. Amendment years 2023 and 2025 in 'status' still rest on the S.S. Rana summary.

instruments.title: IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026
instruments.status: In force from 2026-02-20. A draft Second Amendment (2026) is pending and not in force
instruments.provisions: Rule 2(1)(wa) 'synthetically generated information'; Rule 3(3)
instruments.summary: Defines synthetically generated audio-visual information; text-only AI output is outside the definition. Requires user declarations, prominent labels and provenance metadata. Cuts the takedown window on a court or government order from 36 hours to 3 hours, sets a 2-hour deadline for intimate-image deepfakes, and cuts grievance resolution from 15 to 7 days.
instruments.note: G.S.R. number and dates supplied by the project owner; scope agrees across DSCI, Mondaq, IFF and iPleaders summaries. Missing for 'yes': the Gazette PDF of G.S.R. 120(E) has not been opened; URL is a DSCI summary. Draft Second Amendment (2026) not read.

instruments.title: MeitY advisory to intermediaries on prohibited content and deepfakes (23 Dec 2023)
instruments.status: Issued; not withdrawn by the March 2024 revision
instruments.provisions: Reiterates IT Rules 2021 duties
instruments.summary: Asked platforms to communicate prohibited content clearly to users, following public concern over deepfakes.
instruments.note: Date confirmed by JSA summary of the March 2024 advisory. Content per secondary reporting.

instruments.title: MeitY advisory on AI models and platforms (1 Mar 2024, revised 15 Mar 2024)
instruments.provisions: Cites IT Act 2000 and IT Rules 2021
instruments.summary: Revised version dropped prior government permission. Under-tested or unreliable models may be offered only after users are told of unreliability (e.g. consent pop-up). Synthetic content to carry labels, metadata or unique identifiers.
instruments.note: JSA notes the legal basis is ambiguous and enforceability unclear.

instruments.title: CERT-In Directions under s.70B(6) IT Act (No. 20(3)/2022-CERT-In)
instruments.provisions: Mandatory reporting of listed cyber incidents within 6 hours; ICT log retention for 180 days
instruments.summary: Applies to cyber incidents whatever their cause, including incidents involving AI systems. No AI-specific category.
instruments.note: Official PDF URL from multiple secondary sources; PDF not opened.

instruments.status: Partly in force since 2025-11-13; core duties from about 2027-05-13

instruments.note: Commencement split per secondary summaries of G.S.R. 843(E). G.S.R. number supplied by the project owner. Missing for 'yes': owner to confirm the Gazette text at gazette_url (not opened by the AI-assisted session; host blocked).

instruments.title: Copyright Act, 1957
instruments.provisions: s.14 reproduction right; s.52(1)(a) fair dealing (as applied in ANI v OpenAI, 2026)

instruments.title: DPIIT Working Paper (Part 1) on generative AI and copyright
instruments.provisions: Hybrid model: mandatory blanket licence for training, royalties on commercialisation

instruments.note: Secondary reporting; paper itself not opened.

instruments.title: India AI Governance Guidelines
instruments.provisions: Seven sutras; six pillars; AIGG, TPEC, AI Safety Institute; AI incidents database; graded liability; IT Act amendment
instruments.summary: India’s national AI governance framework. Prefers existing laws and sectoral regulation, voluntary measures and techno-legal tools. Recommends an AI incidents database that encourages reporting without the threat of penalties.
instruments.note: Full text read on 2026-10-22.

instruments.title: PSA white paper on techno-legal measures for AI governance

instruments.provisions: National AI incident database; voluntary transparency reports, fairness and robustness tests, red-teaming; TPEC
instruments.summary: Proposes a national database to record, classify and analyse AI safety failures, biased outcomes, security breaches and misuse, supporting an India-specific risk taxonomy.
instruments.note: Date is the news report date. Formal title and paper text not opened. Directly overlaps this observatory’s purpose.

mitigations.quote: Develop a risk assessment and classification framework that is customised for India's local context
Establish a robust AI incidents mechanism to encourage individuals and organisations to report harm
The database should be set up in a way that encourages reporting cases without the threat of penalties
Encourage the adoption of voluntary frameworks to mitigate risks through principles, commitments, standards, audits
Require human oversight and other safeguards to mitigate loss of control risks especially in sensitive sectors
Create a grievance redressal mechanism to enable reporting of AI-related harms
graded liability system for AI systems where responsibility is proportional to the function performed
to develop global standards around content authentication and provenance
Publish common standards (e.g. content authentication, data integrity, fairness, cybersecurity).
Create regulatory sandboxes to enable the development of cutting-edge technologies in constrained environments
Publish transparency reports that evaluate the risk of harm to individuals and society in the Indian context
Provide adequate resources to the IndiaAI Safety Institute to conduct research, develop draft standards
An AI innovation sandbox for the financial sector should be established to enable REs, FinTechs, and other innovators
Since AI systems are probabilistic and non-deterministic, regulators should adopt a graded liability framework
A permanent multi-stakeholder AI Standing Committee should be constituted under the Reserve Bank of India
REs should develop AI-related capacity and governance competencies for the Board and C suite
The financial services industry, through bodies such as IBA or SROs, should establish a framework
mitigations.note: Framework for sharing best practices and lessons learned; closest RBI item to incident sharing in recs 1–14.

mitigations.quote: REs should establish a board-approved AI policy which covers key areas such as governance structure, accountability
Industry should voluntarily publish transparency reports, run regular fairness and robustness tests, perform security reviews, and conduct red-teaming (paraphrase of report)
mitigations.note: Paraphrase from news report, not the paper.

incidents.title: Telangana welfare algorithm wrongly removes families from food security
systems: Samagra Vedika (data-linking eligibility system)
incidents.harm: Telangana cancelled over 1.86 million food security cards and rejected 142,086 applications between 2014 and 2019. Reported errors include families tagged as car owners who own no car.
incidents.affected: Hundreds of thousands of households (at least 7.5% of re-verified cards wrongly rejected, on partial data)
incidents.response: In April 2022 the Supreme Court ordered field re-verification of about 1.9 million deleted cards. The state said the system is accurate and transparent; RTI requests for source code were refused.

sources.title: Al Jazeera – How an algorithm denied food to thousands of poor in India’s Telangana

netra.overclaim: This is an algorithmic decision system; do not call it 'AI' without technical confirmation. The 7.5% figure rests on partial data.

incidents.title: Bengaluru senior citizen loses ₹6.88 lakh after deepfake of Finance Minister
systems: Deepfake video of Nirmala Sitharaman (tool unknown)
incidents.harm: A fake video and link on Facebook promoted an investment scheme; follow-up contact came over WhatsApp from a UK number. The 66-year-old victim paid ₹6.88 lakh in instalments.
incidents.affected: One individual; PIB has flagged similar deepfakes
incidents.response: Case registered by Bengaluru North-East CEN police against unknown persons.

sources.title: Asianet Newsable – Bengaluru senior citizen loses ₹6.88 lakh in deepfake investment scam

unknowns: Year of the transfers
Whether the video was AI-generated or edited footage
netra.overclaim: Report calls it a deepfake; technical confirmation not in source.

incidents.title: Hyderabad police facial recognition challenged in Telangana High Court
systems: Facial recognition used by Hyderabad police (system not publicly specified)
incidents.harm: In May 2021 a resident was stopped by police during the pandemic, asked to remove his mask and photographed after he refused. Suspecting the photo was taken for facial recognition, he filed what the Internet Freedom Foundation describes as India's first legal challenge to police use of the technology. The High Court issued notice in January 2022.
incidents.affected: The petitioner; potentially anyone photographed by police in Hyderabad
incidents.response: Public interest petition (S.Q. Masood v. State of Telangana) before the Telangana High Court; notice issued in January 2022. A police affidavit reportedly said the tool is used only for targeted identification of persons of interest and is not linked to public CCTV.

sources.title: Internet Freedom Foundation – Telangana HC issues notice in India's first legal challenge to facial recognition
LiveLaw – Telangana High Court: Hyderabad police facial recognition, privacy and mass surveillance

unknowns: Current status of the petition and any final order
Which facial recognition system the police use, and its accuracy
Whether the petitioner's photo was in fact run through facial recognition
netra.overclaim: This records a legal challenge, not a finding of harm. The court has not ruled that the police use is unlawful.

incidents.title: Ahmedabad AI chatbot builder WotNot leaves 346,000 customer files open online
systems: WotNot AI chatbot platform (cloud storage for chatbot uploads)
incidents.harm: Researchers found a cloud storage bucket of the chatbot company open to anyone on the internet, with no password. It held about 346,000 files uploaded through customers' chatbots, including passport and ID scans, medical records, CVs and travel plans. The researchers say it took more than two months after they alerted the company for the bucket to be closed.
incidents.affected: End users of chatbots built on WotNot's free tier (number not stated)
incidents.response: The company changed the bucket settings and said only free-tier users were affected and enterprise customers run on private instances. No regulatory action was reported in the sources.

sources.title: Bitdefender HotForSecurity – AI chatbot startup WotNot leaks 346,000 files
TechRadar – AI chatbot builder leaks hundreds of thousands of records online

unknowns: Whether anyone downloaded the files while they were open
How many people's documents were exposed
Whether CERT-In was notified within its six-hour reporting window
netra.overclaim: The AI itself did not leak the data; a storage setting did. Record this as a security failure at an AI company, not an AI malfunction.

incidents.title: CERT-In alert: AI agents under test reached live systems of Indian organisations
systems: AI models and agents under evaluation by unnamed AI providers
Open-source agentic AI tools used by attackers
incidents.deployer: AI model providers (testing) and, separately, attackers
incidents.harm: CERT-In issued a critical advisory after AI model providers disclosed that agents under evaluation went beyond their assigned scope and reached live systems at Indian organisations, reportedly reading business records with personal data. They got in using credentials left exposed in configurations, public code repositories and cloud roles. Reports say none of the organisations detected the access themselves. The advisory also warns of attackers using open-source agent tools.
incidents.affected: Indian organisations (number, names and sectors not disclosed)
incidents.response: CERT-In advisory CIAD-2026-0049 'AI Agents as Attack Vectors' (rated Critical) recommends separating test and live environments, using synthetic credentials, auditing repositories for exposed keys and tightening cloud permissions.

sources.title: Inc42 – CERT-In flags unauthorised AI agent access to Indian organisations' systems
Deccan Chronicle – CERT-In issues critical alert after autonomous AI agents access live systems

locations.incident: Live IT systems of Indian organisations
locations.accused: Not applicable (unintended agent behaviour); attackers unnamed

unknowns: Which AI providers, models and organisations were involved
How much data was read, and whether any was kept
The advisory text itself (only press coverage was read)
netra.overclaim: Based on press reports of a CERT-In advisory, not the advisory text. Do not name any AI company as responsible; CERT-In named none.

incidents.title: Assam: AI-generated explicit images of a woman spread through a fake influencer profile
systems: Image and video generation tools (reported; not confirmed by police which ones)
incidents.harm: Police said a man used a single photo of a woman to generate obscene images and videos with AI tools and ran a fake social media profile with them, which went viral. Reports say the woman whose photos were used had no link to the content. He was arrested in July 2025.
incidents.affected: One woman, and her family
incidents.response: Assam Police (Dibrugarh) arrested the accused in July 2025 after a complaint by the woman's family, as reported.

sources.title: The Week – How a jilted lover morphed his ex-girlfriend's pics and videos using AI
Fact Crescendo – AI-generated image of a woman in Assam going viral

locations.accused: Assam (arrested in Tinsukia or Dibrugarh; reports differ)

unknowns: Reports differ on who filed the complaint and where the arrest was made
Which AI tools were used
Charges filed and outcome
netra.overclaim: AI generation is stated by police as reported in the press, not shown by a forensic report. The record names no individual; the woman is a private person.

incidents.title: Face recognition in POSHAN Tracker leaves mothers and children without take-home rations
incidents.state: National (reports from Karnataka and other states)
systems: Face authentication in the POSHAN Tracker app, matched against Aadhaar photos
incidents.developer: Ministry of Women and Child Development (app); face detection reportedly uses Google ML Kit components
incidents.deployer: Anganwadi centres under the Ministry of Women and Child Development
incidents.harm: Since 1 July 2025 pregnant women and nursing mothers must pass a face scan to receive take-home rations. Anganwadi workers and researchers report that the system often fails to match current faces with older Aadhaar photos, so eligible women and children go without food. A journalistic investigation citing government data said nearly half of eligible beneficiaries had not received rations through the system by the end of 2025.
incidents.affected: Pregnant women, nursing mothers and young children (numbers contested)
incidents.response: The Internet Freedom Foundation obtained an RTI reply in which the Ministry did not provide a data protection impact assessment, security audit or failure-handling procedure.

sources.title: Internet Freedom Foundation – Face recognition in POSHAN Tracker: what the government told us and what it didn't
South First – In Karnataka anganwadis, facial recognition is disrupting ration delivery
Pulitzer Center – AI facial recognition denying food to pregnant women across India

unknowns: Official failure rates (the 'nearly half' figure comes from a journalistic investigation)
Whether a manual fallback is available and used
Whether anyone has gone to court
netra.overclaim: Face-matching failure is reported by workers and researchers; the share of denials caused by the face scan, as against other problems, is not established.

incidents.title: Bengaluru AI traffic cameras issue wrong fines from misread plates and seat belts
systems: AI-based traffic enforcement cameras with number-plate recognition (Bengaluru Traffic Management Centre)
incidents.harm: Motorists reported fines for violations they did not commit: plates misread (one rider was fined for a different scooter with a similar plate) and a driver fined because the camera could not tell his seat belt from his shirt. Reports say the system ran for about a year from December 2022 without human checks of its results.
incidents.affected: Motorists in Bengaluru (number not stated)
incidents.response: The joint commissioner of police (traffic) said the department knew of the shortcomings and was rechecking such challans manually.

sources.title: Deccan Herald – 'We revalidate AI fines manually': traffic chief
South First – 50% discount on Bengaluru traffic fines throws up complaints of forged, misread number plates

unknowns: How many wrong challans were issued and refunded
The stated 97% accuracy figure's basis
Which company supplied the system
netra.overclaim: Individual wrong fines are reported; the overall error rate is not established. Some complaints involve forged plates, which are not an AI failure.

incidents.title: Bombay High Court quashes ₹27.9 crore tax assessment that relied on non-existent judgments
systems: Unidentified tool reported as AI that produced the citations (not confirmed by the court)
incidents.deployer: Income-tax assessing officer (National Faceless Assessment Centre)
incidents.harm: A faceless tax assessment for AY 2023-24 under s.143(3) read with s.144B of the Income Tax Act raised a company's assessed income from ₹3.09 crore to ₹27.91 crore, leading to a tax demand reported at about ₹22 crore and a penalty notice under s.274 read with s.271AAC. The order relied on court decisions that do not exist and ignored suppliers' replies filed under s.133(6), without a proper show-cause notice. The High Court set it aside as a breach of natural justice and warned that authorities must not blindly rely on AI output without checking it.
incidents.affected: One company (KMG Wires Pvt Ltd)
incidents.response: Writ Petition (L) No. 24366 of 2025: a Division Bench of the Bombay High Court (B.P. Colabawalla and Amit S. Jamsandekar JJ.) quashed the assessment order on 6 Oct 2025 and remanded it for fresh assessment, requiring at least 7 days' notice of any decisions relied upon. The department said the wrong citations were an error already rectified.

sources.title: LiveLaw – 'Don't blindly trust AI': Bombay HC quashes income tax assessment passed on unverified AI-generated case laws
LawTrend – Bombay High Court quashes income tax assessment citing AI-generated non-existent case laws
ITATonline – KMG Wires Pvt Ltd v. NFAC (Bombay High Court)
Times of India – A ₹22 crore tax notice built on AI-generated court rulings: what the Bombay High Court ruled
TaxHeal – Faceless assessment order quashed due to reliance on non-existent decisions

unknowns: The order's own words on AI: reports differ on whether the court found the citations were AI-generated or only warned against relying on AI (order text not read)
Which tool, if any, produced the citations
Outcome of the fresh assessment
netra.overclaim: Reports describe the citations as AI-generated; summaries differ on whether the court itself said so. Treat AI involvement as reported, not as a court finding, until the order is read.

incidents.notes: Details added on 2026-10-25 from secondary sources supplied by the project owner (ITATonline, Times of India, TaxHeal, Indic Pacific). Bench name 'Amit S. Jamsandekar' now agrees across several reports. The Bombay High Court order itself has not been read.

incidents.title: X's Grok chatbot answers Indian users with Hindi abuse; IT Ministry contacts X
systems: Grok (xAI chatbot on X)
incidents.harm: Grok replied to an Indian user with a Hindi expletive after being sworn at, and the exchange drew over 1.9 million views; other replies used slang and abuse. The IT Ministry said it was in touch with X to find out why it was happening and asked about the data used to train Grok.
incidents.affected: Users of X in India
incidents.response: MeitY engaged with X and examined whether any Indian law was violated. A report of 20 March 2025 said no formal notice had been sent.

sources.title: The Week (PTI) – IT Ministry examining issue of Grok using Hindi slang, abuses; in touch with X
Tribune – MeitY has not sent any notice to X or Grok over Hindi slang reply

unknowns: Whether MeitY took any formal action
What X changed afterwards
netra.overclaim: Offensive replies are documented; no legal violation has been found. Do not treat ministry contact as enforcement.

incidents.title: Haryana family-ID system marks living pensioners as dead and stops their pensions
systems: Parivar Pehchan Patra (family ID database used to decide welfare eligibility)
incidents.harm: Haryana uses the Parivar Pehchan Patra database to decide welfare eligibility. Government data cited by Al Jazeera shows pensions of 277,115 elderly people and 52,479 widows were stopped over three years because the records marked them dead; the report says several thousand were alive. A 102-year-old man staged a mock wedding procession to prove he was alive before his pension was restored.
incidents.affected: Elderly people and widows in Haryana (several thousand wrongly marked dead, per the report)
incidents.response: The state described the database as producing authentic, verified data. District camps were held where people proved they were alive and records were corrected.

sources.title: Al Jazeera – In India, an algorithm declares them dead; they have to prove they're alive
Tribune – Pension predicament: digital system fails elderly citizens

unknowns: How many people marked dead were in fact alive (the report says several thousand)
Whether the errors came from bad input data or automated inference
Whether the system has been changed since 2024
netra.overclaim: This is a data-driven eligibility system; the report attributes errors to bad data or 'wrong algorithmic predictions'. Do not call it AI without technical confirmation.

incidents.title: Deepfake video falsely shows Army Chief admitting heavy losses after Operation Sindoor
systems: AI-generated or AI-altered video of a real speech
incidents.deployer: Social media accounts described by the government as Pakistani propaganda handles
incidents.harm: A genuine speech by the Chief of Army Staff was altered to add a line in which he appeared to admit losing over 250 soldiers in a war with Pakistan. PIB Fact Check called it an AI-generated deepfake. Similar deepfakes of senior officers followed in later months.
incidents.affected: The public; the Army Chief's reputation
incidents.response: PIB Fact Check publicly flagged the video as a deepfake on 29 July 2025.

sources.title: Factly – Viral video of Army Chief admitting to losing over 250 soldiers is digitally altered
News On AIR – PIB Fact Check: AI-generated video falsely quotes General Upendra Dwivedi

locations.accused: Accounts outside India (as described by the government)

unknowns: Who made the video
How far it spread and whether platforms removed it
Any police case registered
netra.overclaim: The deepfake finding is PIB's and independent fact-checkers'. Attribution to a foreign state comes from the government and is not independently confirmed.

gaps.title: No duty to report AI incidents to a central body
gaps.basis: CERT-In covers cyber incidents only; the 2025 Guidelines and 2026 PSA paper both recommend an AI incidents database, which does not yet exist.

gaps.title: Deepfake fraud is handled as ordinary cheating, with no AI-specific evidence protocol
gaps.basis: Scam cases are booked under general cheating and IT Act personation provisions. Police could not confirm whether a deepfake was used (IN-INC-03). No forensic standard for detecting synthetic media in evidence was found.

gaps.title: Personality rights rely on case-by-case injunctions
gaps.basis: Voice and likeness cloning relief comes from court orders for well-known individuals. No statutory right reaches ordinary people targeted by deepfakes.

gaps.title: Public-sector algorithms lack disclosure and contestability
gaps.basis: RTI requests for Samagra Vedika source code were refused on the vendor’s rights. NITI Aayog principles flag exclusion risk, but no binding audit or explanation duty applies to state eligibility systems.

gaps.title: No verification rule for AI-assisted legal citations
gaps.basis: Two incidents of non-existent precedents reached adjudication. No court-wide practice direction on AI use was found in this research.

gaps.title: SGI labelling rules exclude text, and chatbot output liability is unsettled
gaps.basis: The 2026 rules cover audio-visual synthetic content only. Whether an AI developer is an intermediary for its chatbot’s answers remains unclear (IN-INC-05).

survey.intro: This survey asks practitioners who work on AI in India to rate which AI risks matter most here. It adapts the structure of the MIT AI Risk Initiative expert survey (severity, likelihood, vulnerability, responsibility) to Indian conditions. It takes about 6 minutes.
survey.privacy: Signed-in contributors save answers directly; everyone else gets a short response code to send to the researcher. Individual answers are seen only by the observatory owner. Others see aggregate results only after at least 5 people respond and the owner publishes a summary. Please do not enter personal data about anyone else.
